questions.prompt: How many rounds does a tree reduction of 1,024 values take?
questions.explanation: log₂ 1024 = 10, with 1,023 additions in total, the same as a loop.

questions.prompt: Why is sequential addressing (stride n/2, n/4, …) faster than interleaved addressing (stride 1, 2, 4, …) in shared memory?
options: Active threads are contiguous, so warps don't diverge and lanes hit consecutive banks
questions.explanation: Same math; better mapping onto warps and banks.

questions.prompt: What does __shfl_down_sync(0xffffffff, v, 4) return in lane 3?
questions.explanation: The value from the lane 4 places higher.

questions.prompt: Why do fast reductions give each thread many elements (a grid-stride loop) rather than one?
options: It keeps the launch at machine size, does most of the work in coalesced registers-only loops, and shrinks the tree overhead
Shuffles only work on large arrays
questions.explanation: The tree becomes a tiny fraction of the work, and the main loop runs at bandwidth.

questions.prompt: Summing the same floats with a tree instead of a loop gives a result that differs in the last bit. Why?
options: Floating-point addition isn't exactly associative, so a different order rounds differently
Shared memory stores at lower precision
questions.explanation: Different summation orders round differently. That's expected.

questions.prompt: Which are valid ways to combine per-block partial sums into one result?
options: Write partials, then run a second small kernel
atomicAdd each block's partial into the result
Have every block read every other block's shared memory
questions.explanation: Blocks can't see each other's shared memory, and __syncthreads() only synchronises one block.
